name: Routines, Schedules, and Social Stories
title: Routines, Schedules, and Social Stories
answer: Routines, schedules, and social stories are visual and written supports that help young children, especially those with autism or anxiety, know what comes next and handle new experiences. Teachers can build them quickly with tools like Boardmaker and Canva for Education, and AI can draft the words. They matter because they reduce uncertainty for children and give families simple, low cost supports that can be used at home.

sections.body: Young children cope better when they can predict what happens next, and picture schedules, visual routines, and short social stories give them that predictability. A social story explains a new or difficult experience, such as a fire drill, a new classmate, or a visit to the dentist, in a way a young child can understand. These supports are especially helpful for children with autism or anxiety, who may find unexpected events particularly hard. The problem they solve is the distress and confusion that comes from not knowing what to expect. Tools such as Boardmaker and Canva for Education let teachers make them quickly, and general AI tools can draft the wording, so a story can be ready the same day it is needed.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In preschool through second grade, the teacher tailors each routine, schedule, or story to the individual child or to the whole class. A social story should use simple, positive language, describe what will happen and how the child might feel, and suggest what the child can do. Because AI drafts often need to be shortened and softened for this age group, the teacher edits them before use. When a story is written for a specific child, the special education teacher or counselor should review it. Visual supports also travel home, for example a picture routine for getting ready in the morning or going to bed, translated into the family's language, and these can be updated whenever a routine changes.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not present a study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It reports that young children do better when they know what comes next and that visual and story supports help many children, especially those with autism or anxiety. It also notes that families often say these small supports make the biggest difference at home. On the text as given, this idea rests on practice and practitioner observation rather than on cited research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher remains responsible for tailoring every routine, schedule, and story to the child or class, and AI drafts are only a starting point. Drafts often need to be shortened and softened for young children, so they should not be used as written. Any story written for a specific child should be reviewed by the special education teacher or counselor before it is used. The text also notes that these supports cost almost nothing to make and can be updated whenever a routine changes, which keeps the decision about when and how to revise them with the school and family.
